opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most exciting and still underexplored directions in machine learning right now.

Think about where we are. There are hundreds of thousands, by now probably millions, of trained models sitting on Hugging Face and similar hubs. Each one is the result of a lot of compute, data, and optimization. But we mostly treat them as black boxes: we download one, run inference, maybe fine-tune it. What we rarely do is look at the weights themselves as data, as a modality you can learn from, the same way we learn from images, text, or audio.

When you do that, a few possibilities open up.

The first is **model analysis**. If you train a representation learner on a large population of models, what we call a model zoo, you can start predicting properties of a model just from its weights, without running it on any data. How well will it generalize? What hyperparameters was it trained with? Is it at an early or late stage of training? Has it been tampered with or backdoored? That's useful for auditing and model selection, especially when you don't have access to the original training data.

The second is **generation**. If you learn a good latent space over weights, which we've called hyper-representations, you can sample from it and produce new models. We've used that to generate initializations that train faster or transfer better than random initialization. You're basically distilling the knowledge of a whole population of models into a generative prior over weights.

Third, there's a more **scientific angle**. Treating weights as a modality lets us study the structure of the weight space itself: how training trajectories look, what symmetries exist, like permutation symmetries between neurons, and how different architectures and datasets shape what gets learned. That says something about why neural networks work, not just whether they work.

Of course, there are real challenges. Weights are high-dimensional, they have those symmetries you need to respect or augment for, and models differ in architecture and size, so building something that generalizes across the zoo is hard. We've also needed to build and release model zoo datasets, because the field didn't have standardized benchmarks for this kind of work.

But the long-term vision is quite compelling: a kind of foundation model for neural network weights, something that understands models the way language models understand text. That could change how we search for, compose, repair, and reuse models, and given how much compute goes into training them, being able to reuse that knowledge more intelligently matters a lot, also from a sustainability perspective.

r001.rationale: It says a learned latent space over weights can generate new models and initializations that train faster than random initialization.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting a model’s properties directly from its weights, including generalization, training settings, and tampering, without running it on data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be here. So the way I like to frame it is this: we have, at this point, millions of trained neural networks sitting in repositories like Hugging Face, and every one of them is essentially a compressed artifact of a learning process. The weights encode what the model learned, how it was trained, what data it saw, which hyperparameters were used. And yet we almost never look at the weights themselves. We treat a model as a black box that we query with inputs and read outputs from. The idea behind treating weights as an input modality, what we sometimes call "weight space learning," is to turn that around and say: the weights are data. Let's learn from them directly.

Once you take that view, a lot of possibilities open up. The first one, and the one we started with, is what you might call model analysis or model forensics. If I give you a trained network, can you predict, just from its weights, how accurate it is on its test set? Can you tell me whether it was trained with a large learning rate or a small one, what the dropout was, whether it's going to generalize well? In our work on "model zoos," where we trained thousands of small networks under controlled conditions, we found that these properties are surprisingly predictable from the weights alone. You can train a hypernetwork, or a simple probe, that reads the weights and tells you things about the model that would otherwise require you to run it on data. That's useful for auditing, for model selection, for detecting things like backdoors or adversarial fine-tuning.

The second direction is representation learning on weights. In the same way we learn embeddings of images or text, we can learn an embedding of a model. Neural networks have this nasty property that the same function can be represented by many different weight configurations, because you can permute neurons in a layer and get an identical model. So a lot of the technical work is about building architectures that are equivariant or invariant to those symmetries, so that two models that compute the same function land near each other in embedding space. Once you have that, you can do things like cluster models, measure similarity between them, find the lineage of a fine-tuned model, and so on.

And then the third, and I think the most exciting, is generative modeling of weights. If you can embed weights, you can also decode from that space, which means you can sample new models. We've shown that you can train a generative model on a population of trained networks and then generate new weights that work out of the box, or that serve as a much better initialization than random. So you can imagine a future where instead of training from scratch, you ask a generator for a model with certain properties, maybe for a certain task or dataset, and you get a starting point that already encodes a lot of what the population has learned. That connects to things like meta-learning and transfer learning, but it approaches them from the weight side rather than the data side.

Now, the honest caveat is scale. Most of what we've done so far is on relatively small models, because a model with billions of parameters is an enormous input, and you can't just flatten it into a vector and feed it to a transformer. So a lot of the open research is about how to tokenize weights, how to exploit structure, whether you work on LoRA adapters instead of full models, and how to make these methods work on the kinds of networks people actually use in production. But I think the broader shift, seeing trained models as a new kind of data with its own structure, is going to matter a lot as the number of models in the world keeps growing much faster than our ability to evaluate each one by hand.

r001.rationale: The response describes generating weights for a model with a specified task and says this could provide a useful starting point instead of training from scratch.

r002.rationale: It describes analyzing a given network’s weights to predict accuracy, training settings, and generalization, supporting model forensics and auditing.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that the weights themselves become data. Normally, we look at a neural network as a function: you put an image in, you get a prediction out. But after training, its parameters also contain information about what it has learned. Can we learn to read that information directly?

Imagine taking a collection of trained networks and learning a representation of their weights. You could use that representation to predict properties of a model—how well it might perform, whether it might generalize to another task, or which models would be useful starting points for adaptation. And if you can learn a useful representation, you can also start asking generative questions: could we generate parameters that give a new network a better initialization?

The challenge is that weights are not a straightforward modality. Two networks can implement the same function while having different parameter arrangements. For example, you can permute hidden units and compensate in the next layer without changing the output. So a useful representation has to account for those symmetries, rather than treating every numerical difference as a meaningful difference.

That’s the direction I find interesting: learning across a population of trained models, with the models themselves becoming the objects we study.

r001.rationale: The response mentions generating parameters for a better initialization and models useful for adaptation, but does not say this would generate weights for a particular task faster.

r002.rationale: The response describes learning representations to predict model properties, but does not clearly identify more precise analysis of an unfamiliar network’s weights.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that the trained network itself becomes a data point. Usually, we look at the data going into a network and the predictions coming out. But the weights encode something about what the network has learned, and we can ask whether we can learn to read that information directly.

Imagine you have a collection of trained networks. Could you build a representation of them that tells you which ones perform similar tasks, which ones generalize well, or which one would be a good starting point for a new problem? That could make model search and transfer learning much more efficient. You might also use that representation to identify unusual models or to guide the generation of new weights.

The challenge is that weights aren't a straightforward description of behavior. Two networks can implement the same function with quite different weight configurations—for example, because you can permute neurons without changing the output. So you need representations that account for those symmetries. But if we can do that, we have a way of learning across models, rather than learning each task from scratch.

r001.rationale: It mentions guiding the generation of new weights and making model search and transfer learning more efficient, but does not clearly connect faster generation to a particular task.

r002.rationale: It describes reading information from weights and identifying unusual models, but does not clearly say this enables more precise analysis of an unfamiliar network’s weights.
